extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students learning the inductive/scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on analysing causation, designing observation and experiment, and determining when phenomena admit deductive prediction versus requiring specific empirical trials. Emphasises decomposition of complex facts, composition of causes, and limits of deductive reasoning in chemistry, physiology and life-sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unjustified generalization from a single peculiar phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer that because volition causes one particular phenomenon (our own actions), volition therefore causes all natural phenomena; only infer common causes when the phenomena 'manifest it by the same sort of indications' and 'conform to the same laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page uses the Volition Theory critique: a cause should only be ascribed across phenomena when their laws bear resemblance. Beware of extending conclusions beyond their grounds merely because one phenomenon exhibits a property (example: we should not conclude earth or fire possess life because some phenomena superficially resemble living actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes (additive composition principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several agents operate jointly, the joint effect is identical with the sum of their separate effects if the same law expressing each separate effect continues to express the part due to that cause in combination. (Called the Composition of Causes.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is typical of mechanical phenomena (e.g., vector addition of forces). If it holds, joint effects can often be predicted deductively from known laws of separate causes; use it where laws are preserved under combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect heteropathic combinations (emergent/transformative effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize cases where the joint action of causes produces effects heterogeneous to the separate effects—where combination yields new phenomena governed by different laws (e.g., chemical combination producing a new substance, or the emergence of life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such heteropathic cases deductive prediction from component laws fails; these require specific experiment and induction to discover the new governing laws. Examples: water from hydrogen and oxygen, biological functions from inorganic parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether deduction or experiment is appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If the law governing each cause separately continues to operate in combination, one may predict the combined effect a priori; if combination alters the laws, experimental trial is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply deductive reasoning in mechanical/compositional domains; prefer experiment and induction in chemical, physiological, and complex-organizational cases where new laws can appear upon combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of effects to causes is conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that effects are proportional to their causes is a particular case of Composition of Causes and holds only where causes are homogeneous and composition applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply proportionality where augmenting a cause changes the kind of effect (e.g., heating: slight heat increases bulk, more heat melts, still more decomposes). Recognize limits and test for points where law changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some laws generated by combinations may themselves compose
rubrics_metrics.description: Heteropathic laws (those arising when components combine) may, in turn, be composable with one another and with original physical laws, allowing higher-level deductive reasoning once those new laws are discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for and attempt to induce intermediate-level laws (e.g., laws of life or chemistry) from repeated combinations; these may permit later deduction for more complex phenomena (Dalton's law of definite proportions, Berthollet's observations, isomorphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no class of phenomena utterly exempt from composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Composition of Causes is not universal, 'there is no class of phenomena in which the Composition of Causes does not obtain' at least in some respects—some properties remain additive (e.g., weight), and some laws persist in combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing a system, identify which properties/laws are preserved under combination and which are altered; this mixed character guides what can be deduced vs what must be discovered experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation as analytical decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation is not merely seeing what is before the eyes but 'seeing what parts that thing is composed of'—resolving complex facts into component antecedents and consequents is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a mental partition (analysis) to identify distinct antecedents and consequents, then attempt to separate them in nature (by experiment) to assign causes to effects. Good observation is a trained skill; rules for observing are rules for preparing the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from inference and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid setting down what one imagines or infers as if it were observed; do not confuse kind of circumstances with their quantities or degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record objectively: note kinds of circumstances and accurately estimate their degrees. Be aware that different observers vary widely in attentiveness, tendency to infer, and granularity of decomposition—train to minimize these errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and training of the observer's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for observing are primarily instructions for self-education: they do not directly teach the act of observation but prepare one's mental faculties to observe and invent well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate attention, habit of decomposing complex wholes, and the ability to detect relevant particulars. Invest in education of observational skills rather than expecting simple procedural rules to suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental separation of antecedents in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine which antecedents are invariably attendant on which consequents, we must effect a separation of facts not only mentally but 'in nature'—i.e., by controlled experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that isolate variables (antecedents) and observe consequent changes; mental analysis must be followed by interventions that separate candidate causes to reveal causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main business of induction: assign causes to effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction's primary goal is to ascertain the laws of causation: determine 'what causes are correctly assigned to what effects, and what effects to what causes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame investigations with the explicit aim of mapping antecedents to consequents; structure observations and experiments to test candidate causal laws and to furnish premises for generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to the scale and purpose in the degree of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessary extent and minuteness of observation and decomposition 'depend on the particular purpose in view'—we need not, nor can we, ascertain the whole universe's state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the granularity of observation and experimental control to the investigative aim; avoid unnecessary detail when the purpose requires coarser facts, but increase resolution when precision matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider chance and spontaneity as possible causal modes (but scrutinize them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and others treated τύχη (chance) and τὸ αὐτομάτον (spontaneity) as efficient causes for some classes of phenomena; modern thought treats such notions cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When causal regularities fail, consider whether chance or spontaneous processes account for variability, but avoid reifying abstract constructs (e.g., treating 'Chance' as a concrete agent) without evidence. Use these as provisional explanatory categories and seek underlying laws where possible.
